title: Growing perennial leek
subtitle: A clump-forming allium that replaces the annual leek harvest with no resowing.
excerpt: Perennial leek produces clusters of small leek-like stems that can be harvested year after year. Divide the clump each autumn and replant to expand the patch. The flavour is mild leek with a hint of garlic.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org). Species information from Agroforestry Research Trust.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small bulb produced in the flowerhead of some alliums instead of, or alongside, seeds. Bulbils fall or can be pulled off and planted to grow new plants. Some perennial leeks and walking onions produce bulbils that are the main means of propagation.

content.text: Perennial leek (Allium ampeloprasum var. babingtonii and related selections) grows in clumps of small, leek-like stems. The flavour is milder than a standard leek, with a slight garlic background. Once established, the plant is self-perpetuating: harvest some stems each autumn and divide the remainder to keep expanding the patch.

Perennial leek grows best in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. It tolerates partial shade but produces smaller stems. In heavy clay, grow in a raised bed or add grit to improve drainage. Hardy to H6 in a sheltered spot.

Harvest individual stems from October to March, cutting at the base. The stems are thinner than a standard leek: use two or three per recipe where one large leek is called for. In spring, lift and divide the clump. Replant sections 20 to 30 cm apart and mulch with compost.
Leave some plants to flower in summer: the flowerheads produce bulbils, which can be collected and planted in August. This is the main way to expand the planting without buying new stock.
